subject: Business Models
title: Unit Economics
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Unit Economics.

hook.text: A single Chick-fil-A averages $8.1 million in revenue. A Subway averages $420,000. Same model, wildly different.

buildup.text: Unit economics measure financial performance of a single franchise location: revenue, costs, profit per store.

discovery.text: Strong unit economics attract better franchisees. Weak ones lead to closures and lawsuits.

twist.text: Franchisors rarely guarantee profitability. You can follow every rule perfectly and still lose money.

climax.text: The gap between top and bottom franchise brands is enormous. Research before investing is not optional.

punchline.text: $8.1M vs $420K per store. Not all franchises are created equal.

quiz.question: What do unit economics measure in franchising?
options: Financial performance of a single location

details.summary: Franchise unit economics measure the profitability of a single franchise location after all costs including royalties, rent, labor, supplies, and marketing..
details.whyItMatters: Most franchise failures result from owners not understanding unit economics before investing. A 500,000-dollar investment generating 50,000 in annual owner income is a 10 percent return that might not justify the risk and work required.
takeaways: Unit economics calculate single-location profit after all franchisor fees and costs
Typical franchise owner income ranges widely from losses to six figures annually
Item 19 FDD data and validation calls with existing franchisees reveal true economics

faq.question: What is a good return on investment for a franchise?
faq.answer: Most financial advisors suggest seeking a franchise where the initial investment can be recouped in 3 to 5 years. This implies 20 to 33 percent cash-on-cash returns. Many franchises take longer, and some never recoup the initial investment at all.

faq.question: How should prospective franchisees evaluate unit economics?
faq.answer: Study the FDD's Item 19 financial data. Call 20 or more existing franchisees to validate real-world numbers. Build a detailed pro forma including all fees, labor, rent, and supplies. Account for owner salary as an expense. Test sensitivity to revenue drops of 10 to 20 percent.
